The example I have for this is a computer keyboard. I would wager everyone who says "I could never play an instrument" uses their keyboard with reasonable proficiency because they are inadvertently practicing every day. If they took an active interest in practicing the keyboard, they would be blind-typing a hundred words per minute in no time and this skill is the exact same skill as any instrument. So my main point is that the learning curve is irrelevant. If you are ready to work hard and spend the hours playing the same section over and over again, you can play anything.

That being said, some instruments certainly require more practice than others. At the top of the list are violin, viola, trumpet, and trombone and all for the same reason: intonation. There is no way to see where your fingers need to go for these instruments. You have to practice and practice until you just know where the note is and it's a lifelong effort. These instruments especially have a very small margin for error, though it's far from impossible. Lots of people play these instruments successfully. I personally relish the challenge.

On the other hand, guitar is an instrument that is quite easy, in my opinion. Thanks to frets, intonation is a non-issue and you can be very lazy with guitar and quickly learn to play a song. There is a much lower time investment before you can make a nice sound with guitar, piano, flute, etc because hitting notes is very "digital" in the sense that you have one note or the next note. There is no infinite number of wrong notes possible between two notes like with the violin. The trade is that the violin family offers the reward of more expression once you learn to navigate intonation. It's the reward for scratching through baa baa black sheep and sounding like you're murdering cats.

The only thing I would specifically mention in regards to trying to choose an instrument is to consider your audience. You sound like me in that you just want to play for yourself. That limits the choice somewhat. For example, a tuba is not the kind of instrument that lends itself to solo play. If you play the tuba, you play a part in an orchestra. You don't sit alone at home playing Paganini on the tuba. When you're looking to play solo music for yourself and family, you want an instrument that can be by itself and still be interesting. These are, in my opinion, the violin family, guitar, and piano, and again, there is a common theme with these instruments: being able to play multiple notes at once. Because a saxophone or flute is somewhat limited to one note at a time, it can be a struggle to produce multiple, really interesting pieces. They are better suited to being in bands and will often require accompaniment. With cello/guitar/piano, you can play chords and two simultaneous parts and this is what makes them such versatile instruments.

A final tip is to pick the one you want to learn over other distracting factors like logic. I remember thinking about learning cello and considering compromising with viola because cellos are so damn expensive. I think that would have been a bad decision at the time. I picked cello because I think it's the best sounding instrument out there and that passion and enjoyment at hearing it is what keeps me interested. I want to practice. No one has to make me. I might not have stuck with the viola had I compromised, though considering I'm learning it now, maybe I would have. So pick the one that really inspires you and don't worry about much else. If you really love the violin, no amount of intonation work or learning curve will stop you. Besides, at the start, you would rent an instrument for a while so you can always change your mind and try something else. Or you could learn all of them!

Be warned, however, once you start practicing an instrument, you will never, ever believe you played something well. The reality of music, I find, is endless self-criticism and always feeling like it should have been better. You'll be chasing that dragon for the rest of your life. I'm chasing it through my fourth instrument! LOL. Seriously, all the best. Music is a great hobby, especially if you like to share. People love music.

Something that I’ve recently started doing is baking, and making my own recipes. I’ve read through a few older cookbooks (written before all recipes called for butter and sugar) to get a reference point of what ingredients usually go in different types of food (and in what quantities) and it’s nice being able to make snacks that are sweet but don’t have too much sugar. I’ll admit that they’re a little janky since I’m living off of a college student budget but it’s interesting what a few spices can do for flavoring.

What’s mind boggling to me is that there’s people out there that would eat the entire batch in a day. The cookies that I made (about 36) lasted a whole week, and that was with sharing them with friends that came over to study. Yet to someone else it’s a light snack. Crazy.

I LOVE old cookbooks! I started collecting them when I was first married, because old cookbooks tend to have real recipes in them--like, normal recipes with regular ingredients, designed for everyday cooking and eating--rather than cookbooks today which tend to have wildly exotic ingredients and be extremely fiddly, designed more for weekend Instagram cooks, if you know what I mean.

I do a ton of baking, as well, so please get in touch if you ever run into any problems or have questions about what to do with certain ingredients or whatever. Baking tends to be pretty self-explanatory, but in the almost-twenty-years that I've been cooking and baking almost every day I've learned a lot of little tricks and such. I also have a lot of recipes that I've come up with or altered myself, so if you are ever looking for something new to do with that chicken or that broccoli or whatever, or your yeast isn't rising properly or whatever...you know who to hit up. :-)

And since most of that time has been a matter of trying to stretch a small food budget as far as possible for a family of four, I have lots of ideas for leftovers or Things To Do With A Pound of Ground Beef or whatever. I once made two pounds of ground beef and a bag of frozen veg last five days, with the addition of a little flour, milk, eggs, potatoes--I made a big pot of beef barley soup, and served it a different way every day: first plain soup, then soup with dumplings, then the met & veg on little rolls with mashed potato, then the meat & veg baked in Yorkshire puddings, then fried mashed potato with the remainder of the soup over it. (We were all a little sick of the soup by the end of that week, but we were also broke, lol, and we still ate, which is what mattered to me.) One night this last week I made a gravy with half a pound of ground beef and served it over/next to baked potatoes. The whole meal was maybe four bucks and it served four people just fine.

And heh, I know what you mean about snack vs. all-week food. I usually make a batch of brownies or a chocolate chip cookie cake or something at the beginning of the week, and it usually lasts until Friday...but I made brownies once for a (fat) guest, a friend of my older daughter's, and watched over half the batch disappear in under an hour. That was eighteen brownies, reduced to seven by the time he left. I had to make another batch the next day so we'd have dessert for the rest of the week. (My brownie recipe is excellent, btw, but unfortunately my attempt to make them with stevia once failed miserably. Sigh. I'm not much for artificial sweeteners, so I wasn't super disappointed, but it would have been nice to reduce those brownies to about 150 calories each instead of the almost 300 they usually are.) And the secret to a chocolate chip cookie cake (or chocolate chip cookies) that will knock everyone's socks off is adding some butterscotch chips. :-) No one notices they're there, really, but the flavor is amazing. I haven't tried using stevia in those, because the amount of sugar is relatively low anyway, but I imagine it would work much better than the brownies did.

Anyway. Lol, I can talk about this stuff all day. I taught my SD to cook, starting when she was 12 (she's 25 now and still has the notebook full of recipes I gave her then), but neither of my daughters have shown any interest, sigh. So I'd be happy to help you, if you ever need it--I don't expect you will, but the offer is there just in case.
